excerpt: Vital For St. Thomas … After a fine first half showing in this Under-12 "C" final in the Coiste Iomana Tournament in Loughrea on Monday, St. Thomas held out for a win. They were awarded a 21-yard free after four minutes and full-back Tony Headd slammed home a goal. In the ninth minute St. Thomas got another free and full-back Headd obliged again with a point. The first real attack by Fohenagh was defied by a great score from Kenneth Larkin. St. Thomas attacked again and Enda McGarry ended it with a great goal to leave St. Thomas leading by 2-1 to 0-0. But for some heroic defending by Sean Moclair they would have stretched their lead even further early in the second half. Fohenagh were at last rewarded when Paul Kennedy got a point after nine minutes of the second half. They picked up their game very much after this and a goal by John Devine brought them closer to St. Thomas after ten minutes of the second half. But they could not get through for the all-important goal. St. Thomas can thank in particular Tony Headd, Sean Fahey, David Quinn, Kevin Smyth, and Justin Flannery. excerpt: A Workmanlike win for Salthill juniors in county semi … THE Salthill hurling team, newly promoted to Junior 'A' status only this season, underlined its potential with a clear, if workmanlike, four point victory over Fohenagh in this county championship quarter final clash at Athenry on Sunday. … A well struck free from Ryan, that went all the way to the net, established a three point lead for Salthill, with only the accuracy of Fohenagh's free taker Gerry Burke — himself a former Salthill player — keeping his side within striking distance against a rearguard in which the reliable full back triumvirate of Joe Greaney, Denis O'Mahoney, and John McGrath were outstanding. Salthill could have found themselves in all kinds of trouble after the resumption when a speculative shot from Tony Kirwan went past Salthill goalkeeper Stephen Cullinane, to narrow the gap to just a point. However, points by Ryan, McGee, and a well-taken Michael Gavin goal midway through the half re-established Salthill's lead. … Full back Micheal Barrett, centre back Colm Kirwan — the team's best player — Seamus Lohan and the evergreen Eugene Hession tried hardest for Fohenagh.

Mochlair, T. Kirwan (0-2), John Devine and A. Madden (0-5, all frees); VANQUISHED team photo names Tony Kirwan, Padraig Leonard, John Devine, Alan Madden and Seamus Mocklair. S. Mochlair / Seamus Mocklair (print) = Séamus Moclair; Padraig Leonard (print) = Pádraic Leonard
excerpt: VANQUISHED ... the Fohenagh side which failed in their bid to win the county junior title for the first time in history when they were defeated by Athenry in the final at Ballinasloe on Sunday. Back row, left to right: Tony Kirwan, Michael Barrett, Gerry Madden, Padraig Leonard, Joe Fallon, Gerry Burke, Seamus Lohan and Padraig Daly. Front row: John Devine, Alan Madden, Colin Kirwan, Noel Higgins, Paul Kennedy, Seamus Mocklair and Michael Coen, Team mascot Daniel Lyons. … Athenry's perfect blend helps secure Junior A hurling title Athenry 1-8 Fohenagh 0-9 by John Fallon BEFORE a ball was ever pucked in this year's junior A hurling championship Athenry, with their blend of experience and youth, were installed as firm favourites for the title. They lived up to that billing at Duggan Park, Ballinasloe, on Sunday but only after they fought off a dogged battle from a Fohenagh side who refused to surrender the chance of their first smidgen of glory since their famous County Cup wins of '59 and '60. Victory would have crowned a great year for Fohenagh. They packed in training after they lost their first two games in this year's championship but got back into the title race with victory in a group play-off which saw them twice beat Salthill. The exploits of Tony Kirwan for the victorious Galway U21 side — and his subsequent elevation onto the senior side — provided a great boost to Fohenagh and they showed great spirit when lowering Castlegar in the semi-finals. But on Sunday they were beaten by the better team with Athenry's experience in crucial positions, coupled with the containment of Kirwan until the closing stages by captain Michael Higgins, proving decisive in an open game of hurling which provided plenty of entertainment for the relatively large crowd. … Fohenagh full-back Colin Kirwan led as a captain should while wing-backs Michael Coen and Gerry Madden had some great moments. Padraig Leonard and Padraig Daly hurled well around the middle of the field but they were unable to stop Declan Higgins' dominance of this area. The containment of Tony Kirwan robbed Fohenagh of their most dangerous forward and while Seamus Lohan, John Devine and Alan Madden threathened with sporadic forays, it was not with the same sort of dash that Kirwan has led the Fohenagh attack all season. … Fohenagh: N. caption: INA snip — Tuam Herald 4 Apr 1942: Fohenagh win the North Board junior final
excerpt: Fohenagh beat Cussaun to win the North Board junior final after an hour of hard, fast hurling. Cussaun's goalie and backs kept them out for ages, and Fohenagh fluffed a few chances by dawdling in front of goal, but two late goals settled it. No score printed.

caption: INA snip — Connacht Tribune 3 Jun 1944: Cussane beat Fohenagh in the delayed 1943 North final

caption: INA snip — Clare Champion 19 Jul 1952: Fohenagh 7-5, Gort 0-3

caption: INA snip — Tuam Herald 30 Aug 1952: Skehana win the 1952 replay
excerpt: After Fohenagh rescued a draw with a last-minute penalty goal, the replay at Castleblakeney was level for a half before Skehana pulled away to win 3-7 to 2-1. The paper calls it a semi-final; the existing wiki row calls the drawn game a final.

caption: INA snip — Westmeath Independent 4 Jul 1953: Fohenagh win the 1953 Kilconnell tournament
excerpt: Fohenagh beat a weak Ballymacward side in the semi-final and then edged Cappatagle No. 2 in a 'thrill-a-minute' final. The Sweeney trio and the Glynn brothers led the way, and a schoolboy goalkeeper named Laly was first-class. No score printed.

caption: Connacht Tribune 3 Oct 1953: Fohenagh 4-7, Claregalway 4-6
excerpt: Fohenagh led 3-6 to 0-4 at the break, then had to hang on as Claregalway came storming back, and the afternoon got so lively that the Gardaí had to help out. Fohenagh squeezed through by a single point, 4-7 to 4-6, with a full team list printed.

caption: Connacht Sentinel 20 Oct 1953: Maree 4-2, Fohenagh 2-3: the 'travesty' at Loughrea
excerpt: Fohenagh led 1-3 to 0-0 at half-time, then Maree hit three quick goals and a Fohenagh goal was ruled out. In the closing minutes the hurleys were swung more like cavemen's clubs than camáin, and the referee gave up trying to line the teams up again. Happily the paper says nobody was seriously hurt. Maree went through 4-2 to 2-3.

caption: INA snip — Connacht Tribune 24 Oct 1953: Maree v Fohenagh report (Tribune reprint)

caption: INA snip — Munster Express 28 May 1948: Waterford paper notes the Fohenagh camogie life ban
excerpt: Even a Waterford columnist heard about it: after followers of the Fohenagh club attacked an umpire at a county tie with St. Grellan's, Ballinasloe, the Galway Camogie Board suspended the team for life. caption: INA snip — Tuam Herald 28 Aug 1948: Fohenagh camogie reinstatement refused
excerpt: Fohenagh asked to be let back in. The National Organiser backed them, but Caltra's delegate objected and the application failed. Someone at the meeting said the rule was 'very hard on the girls', and the Board agreed the trouble was the supporters' behaviour, 'not the girls fault'.

caption: INA snip — Connacht Sentinel 12 May 1942: Claregalway object to the referee (Sentinel, snippet only)

caption: INA snip — Connacht Tribune 16 May 1942: The referee question
excerpt: Claregalway didn't want Mr. Cullen as referee for their semi-final with Fohenagh and threatened to give Fohenagh the match and pull out. One delegate worried that if the Board gave in, 'Fohenagh can come along next week and object again'. The chairman ruled the game would go ahead the next Sunday with Mr. Cullen in charge.

caption: INA snip — Connacht Tribune 13 Jun 1942: Both teams suspended after Athenry
excerpt: The 1941 semi-final at Athenry never finished: spectators poured on, the referee told Fohenagh to leave 'for their own safety', and captain Michael Barrett said he was hit in the mouth and kicked. After two hours of heated talk the Board suspended BOTH clubs for a year and handed the 1941 title to Eyrecourt, who must have been delighted to win a final without lifting a hurley.

excerpt: In 1907 the club elected its parish priest, Fr. Harney, as president, and on 21 January 1907 Fohenagh was re-affiliated to the County Board even though Ahascragh objected strongly. Fr. Harney wrote that the Fohenagh players were 'respectable men' guilty of no 'dishonourable conduct'. A few weeks later the 'Fohena Hurling Club' told the papers it would start practice the very next Sunday.
citeChip: A History of Fohenagh (Tony O'Gorman) · ch.17 · p.140–141
credit: From A History of Fohenagh by Tony O'Gorman

caption: The Battle of Athenry (1942)
excerpt: The Battle of Athenry. Fohenagh met Claregalway in the 1941 county junior semi-final at Athenry in May 1942, and it went about as well as a picnic in a hailstorm. The referee reported that Claregalway spectators rushed onto the pitch and some Fohenagh players were hurt; he could not clear the field, so he called the match off. At the long County Board meeting that followed, captain Mike Barrett said he was assaulted and that the referee had asked him to take his team to safety. Tim Glynn's memory of the day, the book notes with a wink, 'differed slightly with his captain's story of injured innocence!' The referee wanted a replay and Mick Silver proposed a two-year ban for Claregalway, but the chairman, Thomas O'Connor (Claregalway), ruled that 'it takes two to start a fight': both clubs got a year's suspension. Eyrecourt, the East Board winners, were declared county junior champions without needing to puck a ball.
citeChip: A History of Fohenagh (Tony O'Gorman) · ch.17 · p.144–145
credit: From A History of Fohenagh by Tony O'Gorman

caption: The turf lorry and the Athenry Arch (1947)
excerpt: How do you get a camogie crowd 35 miles to Galway in 1947? In Kevin Doherty's (Woodlawn) turf lorry, 'suitably insulated'. The trip home after the county final win is local folklore: the celebrations started early in Foster Street, the driver was in no state to drive, and John Joe Kirwan took the wheel. Then the lorry got wedged in Athenry's medieval Arch! After plenty of advice, the top tier of the creel was taken off, and the lorry and its relieved passengers got home with only one stop, in Menlough.
citeChip: A History of Fohenagh (Tony O'Gorman) · ch.17 · p.146
credit: From A History of Fohenagh by Tony O'Gorman

caption: Seven points up, then the fists came out (1956)
excerpt: Fohenagh led Tynagh by seven points to nil in a Junior A game at Kiltormer on 15 July 1956, until fighting on the pitch got the game called off. Both teams were suspended for twelve months. The book calls it 'a devastating blow', but the County Board still let Fohenagh into senior hurling, and three years later they were county champions.
citeChip: A History of Fohenagh (Tony O'Gorman) · ch.17 · p.148
credit: From A History of Fohenagh by Tony O'Gorman

caption: 1959: ten points down, county champions
excerpt: Fohenagh drew the 1959 county final with Castlegar, then lost two seminarians back to their studies and two more players to injury before the replay. Castlegar led by ten points at half-time. 'Miraculously', Fohenagh won 3-9 to 4-5 and Marty Glynn lifted the County Senior Cup for the first time ever. The party went on and on in the Old School Hall, turned into a bar by Ahascragh supporters.
citeChip: A History of Fohenagh (Tony O'Gorman) · ch.17 · p.149–151
credit: From A History of Fohenagh by Tony O'Gorman

caption: From Fohenagh to Ahascragh/Fohenagh (1999–2002)
excerpt: With fewer children around (96 on the school roll in 1988, 46 by 2000), Fohenagh joined Ahascragh at underage level in 1999, and won county U-14 B and Minor B titles straight away. On 21 January 2002 both clubs held their AGMs at the same time and disbanded, and the new club Ahascragh/Fohenagh was born. For many who remembered the 1950s glory days, losing their 112-year-old club was sad, but there was no other way.
citeChip: A History of Fohenagh (Tony O'Gorman) · ch.17 · p.156–157
credit: From A History of Fohenagh by Tony O'Gorman
